To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Nickel toxicity to Hyalella is highly variable and depends on the source of the sediment.

(1) Ni in overlying waters was a reliable indicator of Ni toxicity in Imhoff settling cone tests with large water to sediment ratios, but not in beaker tests, and (2) Ni body concentrations were a reliable indicator of toxicity in all tests.
Ni toxicity to Hyalella is strongly dependent on the source of sediment, and that toxicity is predicted best by Ni body concentrations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a better understanding of the relationship between Ni bioavailability and chronic toxicity in sediments.
the development and evaluation of methods to predict the effects of metals in aquatic sediments on aquatic organisms.
the development of an ecotoxicological test for nickel in sediments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ni toxicity to Hyalella in sediment is best predicted by body concentrations of Ni, and that the 4-week EC10 is a reasonable threshold concentration for chronic effects.

Ni toxicity to Hyalella in Ni-spiked sediment was not significantly affected by sediment type, and that Ni concentrations in overlying water and Ni concentrations in Hyalella were equally good predictors of Ni toxicity.

Ni is a relatively non-toxic metal to H. azteca, and that the most reliable predictor of Ni toxic effects is the body concentration of Ni in Hyalella, which can be predicted from a sediment-water equilibrium model.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ni in sediments and in the water column can both be important in controlling the toxicity of Ni to benthic invertebrates, but that sediment concentrations provide the best prediction of toxicity.
Ni bioaccumulates to toxic body concentrations in sediments with a low organic carbon content, but is not available to Hyalella in sediments with high organic carbon content.
Ni toxicity in sedentary animals such as Hyalella is strongly affected by the bioavailability of Ni in the sediment.
The main takeaway from our work is that

bioavailability is not the sole factor determining Ni toxicity to Hyalella, but rather that the source of Ni and the test conditions used (e.g., sediment to water ratios and test vessel type) are important factors.
bioavailability of Ni is strongly influenced by sediment characteristics and that toxicity of Ni to Hyalella is strongly influenced by the method used to expose organisms to sediments.
the toxicity of Ni in sediment is highly dependent on the sediment matrix and that the bioavailability of Ni in sediment can be estimated from body concentrations of Hyalella in the same sediment.
